videos.title: Bad Ignition Coil Symptoms: 7 Common Signs
videos.transcript_text:
hey everyone Brian here your honest
mechanic one of the key components in a
vehicle's ignition system is the
ignition coil its job is to step up the
low voltage from the battery to
thousands of volts to create a strong
spark at the spark plug this spark
ignites the air fuel mixture in the
engine cylinders to power the vehicle
over time due to heat vibration and
component wear the ignition coil can
fail leading to issues with the
performance and drivability of your
vehicle let's go over the common signs
and symptoms that can indicate your
ignition coil may be going bad number
one engine misfires this is probably the
most noticeable sign that your ignition
coil could be faulty what happens is
when the coil starts to fail it may cut
in and out randomly unable to provide a
consistent spark to the spark plugs this
causes one or more of the cylinders to
misfire sporadically resulting in rough
idle vibration jerky motion as you drive
and loss of power number two rough idle
if you notice that your engine RPM seems
to fluctuate up and down at stop lights
that's a sign of a potential culprit
being the ignition coil the inconsistent
Sparks make the idle speed rise and fall
randomly number three reduced power and
acceleration since the ignition coil is
responsible for generating the Sparks to
ignite the fuel mix in the engine a bad
one can mean the combustion process
doesn't happen properly this can reduce
the engine's available power used for
acceleration you'll notice the vehicle
feels more sluggish and slow number four
poor fuel economy along with the power
loss A misfiring engine because of a
faulty ignition coil also reduces the
combustion efficiency this usually
translates into more trips to the gas
station because you're burning more fuel
than normal operation number five check
engine light comes on most modern
vehicles Les monitor the ignition and
other major systems with sensors
connected to the onboard computer known
as the powertrain control module or PCM
it can detect issues like engine
misfires and ignition coil faults you'll
likely see it trigger error codes like P
03000 P 0301
p0302 indicating which cylinder is
experiencing misfires number six
difficult vehicle starts because the
coil provides the high voltage for the
spark plugs to ignite the compressed air
fuel mixture on Startup a bad one can
cause hard starts you may notice the
engine cranking over longer than usual
before it finally catches and starts up
rough or uneven sounding and number
seven gasoline smell from exhaust if an
ignition coil completely fails it will
stop sparking the plugs altogether in
that particular cylinder most likely
when this happens you end up with raw
unburnt fuel going right through the
exhaust this manifests as a strong
gasoline odor coming from the tailpipe
along with black smoke in some cases I
hope you found this overview on symptoms
of bad ignition coils helpful let me
know if you have any other questions if
you find this video helpful Please
Subscribe and like

lubrication regular engine oil changes

serious damage over time second over
speeding pushing the engine to rev

third oil starvation if oil supply pipes

not reach the turbo causing extensive
damage fourth oil contamination dirty or

components leading to premature wear and

spin at over a 100,000 RPM any debris

the turbo wheels and Blades these are

symptoms of a failing
turbocharger one of the first signs that
your turbocharger is in trouble is low
engine power if your car doesn't

exhaust smoke is another indicator this

worn turbo SE wheels and into the

wear if you notice a burning oil odor it

issues the engine's computer detects
problems through sensors and triggers
the light a drop in fuel economy is
another symptom a faulty turbo has to
work harder which can hurt your gas
mileage
and lastly look out for oil leaks around
the Turbo from worn seals these symptoms
are telltale signs of a turbocharger on
its last legs in summary common turbo
failure causes are inadequate
lubrication over revving oil starvation
contamination and foreign objects we've
walked through the ins and outs of
turbochargers how they work and the
signs that might indicate yours is on
the fritz we've underscored that low
engine power blue exhaust smoke a
distinct tur turb whistle a burning oil
odor a lit check engine light poor fuel
economy and oil leaks are all symptoms
of a potentially failing turbocharger
but remember prevention is better than
cure regular maintenance and proper
operation are the keys to a Turbocharger
longevity don't push your engine Beyond
its limits change your oil regularly
keep the turbocharger Clean and Free
from foreign objects keep an eye out for
these signs your turbo may be wearing
out if you notice any don't hesitate to
seek professional help and remember a
well-maintained Turbocharger means a
well performing vehicle stay safe and
happy driving

videos.title: Check Injection System Renault: Causes & Fix
videos.transcript_text:
ever had the check injection system
alert pop up in your Renault vehicle in
today's video we'll be tackling this
common issue this alert is a bit of a
catch-all indicating there's a hiccup
with the engine management system more
often than not it's linked to your fuel
injection components we're talking about
things like injectors fuel pumps and so
on the alert basically means that your
renault's computer has detected A Fault
in one or more of its sensors or
components it's like your car is telling
you hey something's not quite right here
it's a heads up that you might need to
take a closer look under the hood but
before you start panicking remember that
this alert can be triggered by a wide
range of issues now that we know what
the alert means let's dive into the
common causes there are several reasons
why Urena might be flashing the check
injection system alert let's go through
them one by one first up is a bad MAP
sensor the map sensor is a critical
component in your car's engine that
monitors the air intake it sends
information to the ECU which then
adjusts the fuel injection timing if the
map sensor is disconnected or has a
faulty electrical connection it could
trigger the check injection system alert
next we have a faulty exhaust pressure
sensor also known as the differential
sensor this little device measures the
gas pressure between the intake and the
exhaust of the particulate filter if
it's malfunctioning it could trick the
ECU into thinking there's a leak in the
exhaust system your car might then go
into limp mode limiting acceleration and
speed the third common cause is a bad
fuel pump though not as common as the
first two if your fuel pump is faulty
and not producing enough pressure to
inject fuel into the engine it could
definitely set off that warning light on
your dash our fourth culprit is dirty
fuel injectors these are the valves that
control how much fuel is injected into
the engine if they're clogged with
carbon deposits they can't inject the
right amount of fuel leading to a power
drop and poor acceleration finally the
last common cause we're going to discuss
is a bad battery a failing battery can
cause a myriad of electric problems and
can also lead to a power loss if your
battery is old it might not be able to
supply enough voltage to run your
vehicle efficiently telltale signs of a
bad battery could be dimming or
flickering lights when you start your
car or random fault messages popping up
so there you have it these are the five
most common causes why your Renault
might be flashing the check injection
system alert understanding the cause is
half the battle now let's talk Solutions
we've identified the possible culprits
now let's examine the solutions to these
common causes of the check injection
system alert first up the bad MAP sensor
in the event of a disconnected or faulty
map sensor you'll need to reconnect it
or replace it this involves opening the
hood locating the sensor inside the
engine and ensuring it's securely
connected to its harness if the sensor
is faulty it's a straightforward swap
with a new one next the faulty exhaust
pressure sensor this sensor is crucial
for your renault's emission control
system if faulty it should be replaced
without delay replacement involves
unplugging the old sensor and installing
a new one a task which can be
accomplished with basic mechanical
skills the third common cause we
discussed was a bad fuel pump if the
fuel pump isn't pumping enough pressure
to inject fuel into the engine it's time
for a replacement this is a more complex
task involving draining and removing the
fuel tank so it might be best to leave
this to a professional mechanic moving
on to dirty fuel injectors if these are
clogged with carbon deposits a good
cleaning can often do the trick there
are several methods to clean fuel
injectors including using a dedicated
fuel injector cleaner that you add to
your fuel tank or having a professional
mechanic perform a more thorough
cleaning service lastly the bad battery
if your battery is causing the issue
it's time to replace it this is a
relatively simple task that most car
owners can handle first you'll
disconnect the old battery and then
install the new one always remember to
disconnect the negative terminal first
to prevent any electrical shorts and
there you have it you're now equipped
with the knowledge to tackle the check
injection system alert in your Renault
vehicle
before we wrap up here's a friendly
reminder to hit that subscribe button
and turn on notifications this way you
won't miss out on our future videos
where we share more helpful tips and
tricks for maintaining your vehicle
we're always here to help you navigate
the sometimes tricky world of car
maintenance with ease and confidence and
don't forget to give this video a thumbs
up if you found it helpful your likes
and comments fuel our motivation to keep
delivering high quality content tailored
to your needs if you have any questions
or suggestions feel free to drop a
comment below we're always eager to hear
from our viewers remember knowledge is
power especially when it comes to car
maintenance thanks for watching stay
safe and happy driving

videos.title: Bad Clutch Master Cylinder Symptoms (Common Signs)
videos.transcript_text:
hey everyone Brian here with the honest
mechanic Channel today I want to talk
about some common symptoms that can
indicate you have a bad or failing
clutch master cylinder this is an
important component in manual
transmission Vehicles which operates the
clutch by pushing fluid into the slave
cylinder disengaging the clutch disc
from the flywheel when you press the
pedal when the clutch master cylinder
starts to fail you'll notice some issues
when trying to change gears and operate
the clutch knowing the signs of a bad
one can help you diagnose the problem
and get it repaired before it leaves you
stranded the number one sign is likely a
soft or spongy feeling clutch pedal when
you go to push the pedal into shift
gears you'll feel like there is a lot of
play or it feels really soft and may go
all the way to the floor this typically
indicates that air has gotten into the
hydraulic lines or the master cylinder
is not building enough pressure properly
you might also find the clutch pedal
itself gets very stiff and difficult to
push almost like the whole mechan
mechanism is gummed up this can happen
when there are blockages or failures
inside the cylinder not allowing fluid
to flow and apply the clutch as intended
another obvious symptom is when you
fully depress the clutch but it sticks
to the floor and won't return back up
after changing gears or using the clutch
the pedal should always come back up and
be ready for you to press it again if
it's stuck down it means hydraulic
pressure isn't releasing and is a sign
of master cylinder problems you may also
have a really hard time actually
shifting years if the clutch isn't
disengaging properly you'll most likely
hear grinding noises every time you try
to put the transmission into the next
gear because the master cylinder isn't
doing its job this makes smooth shifting
difficult and damaging to the gears long
term check underneath your vehicle as
well one clear indicator is leaking
brake fluid around the transmission and
clutch area the seals inside the
cylinder have likely failed and are
allowing hydraulic fluid to escape
leaving you with nothing to apply the
clutch itself you'll probably notice the
Reservoir level getting lower than
normal too and when checking that
Reservoir keep an eye out for dirty or
muddy fluid if it's not a nice clear
color it means the clutch system has a
lot of wear material seal breakdown and
just overall contamination happening I
tend to recommend completely flushing
the system in cases like these to try
and clean things out some other issues
that may come up include noises from the
transmission or clutch pedal area
whenever you try to use the clutch
listen for squeaking grumbling or
grinding noises as you press the pedal
this often indicates internal binding
and wear is present and finally in
really bad cases you might experience
the engine stalling out when trying to
take off from a stop sign or pulling out
into traffic especially if you start to
engage the clutch pedal and it doesn't
fully come back up this shows how
crucial the master cylinder is for
proper manual transmission operation
hopefully this gives you a good overview
of the major symptoms pointing to a
failing clutch master cylinder in your
stick shift vehicle be on the lookout
for spongy pedal feel stuck pedals
leaking fluid gear grinding and anything
unusual happening when operating the
clutch itself if you find this video
helpful Please Subscribe and share

symptoms of bad egr valve
1. engine stalls and run rough while
idling if the egr is stuck in the open
position more exhaust gas goes into the
engine intake making the engine starve
for fresh air
this can make the maf sensor red no air
getting into the engine and thus can
stall at low engine speeds
most of the time the engine struggles to
maintain the idle rpm and suffers more
vibrations or shakes badly
2. low performance from the engine
similar to the first reason if the egr
is stuck at open position it allows more
exhaust gas to enter the engine making
the engine starve for fresh air
while accelerating engine needs more
fresh air to get its peak performance
the more exhaust gas will also alter the
fuel injection rates which will further
decrease the performance reasonably
3. fuel smell around the car
if the egr is not functioning properly
the fuel inside cannot burn efficiently
due to disturbed air-to-fuel ratios
this will emit more unburnt fuel into
the exhaust making a pungent fuel loader
this is most common when the car is
first started or when the engine is cold
4. knocking sound
the prime function of egr is to lower
the combustion temperature
when it's stuck closed it will result in
increased engine cylinder temperature
because the fuel is burned more
efficiently with plenty fresh air
this increase in temperature can make a
knocking sound when go beyond the
manufacturer designed values and
sometimes the engine can overheat
5. fail in emission tests
as the function of egr is to reduce the
combustion temperature which further
reduces the production of nox compounds
which are harmful to the environment
a faulty egr can alter the controlled
combustion and will affect the emission
rates this might be the reason your

6. altered fuel economy a faulty egr
alters the combustion efficiency of the
engine badly and you may need to press
more on the accelerator to go forward
than usual
this can make the overall efficiency of
the engine go down and affects the gas
mileage badly
7. check engine light comes on most
modern cars have electronically
controlled egr systems which has
positioned sensors to detect the
position of the valve
any malfunction of egr is picked up by
the ecm and throws a check engine light
to warn the driver

anybody can throw a brand-new set of
pads on a vehicle but it takes a real
technician to understand the signs of
when you need to replace the brake
caliper the number-one sign well it's
uneven brake pad where if the brake pads
are not allowed to move in the bracket

the force between the two pads that's a
sign that something's hanging up inside
the caliper or some of the hardware is

there you run into a situation where a
caliper guide pin cannot be removed from

for a lot of consternation with a lot of

in there well chances are corrosion is
going to come back this is why you need
to install a new caliper number four
while this is kind of a bonus tip
anytime you're replacing a caliper look
at the brake hose chances are if the

fuel injection precisely this

engine this imbalance can cause improper

notice your car jerking surging or
vibrating while driving especially at a
steady speed or when shifting gears the
second badm AF sensor symptom is a rough
idle like the previous symptom an
incorrect air fuel ratio will cause
rough Idols that is because at lower
speeds or when you're stationary the car
needs more fuel to keep the engine
running but if the MAF sensor suggests a

previously you're in luck however losing

sluggish and unpredictable the fourth
symptom of bad mass airflow sensor is a
stalling engine too much air or too
little Fuel and your car will stall when

costly repair when the engine runs rich
it puts extra strain on the catalytic
converter and replacing it can cost as
much as
$3,500 or more the ninth sign of a bad
MAF sensor is engine knocking if you
hear strange pinging or knocking sounds
from the engine it could be due to an
improper air fuel ratio these noises are
a sign that your engine is struggling to
run smoothly the knocking sound is fuel
burning unevenly in the engine if left
untreated this will end up damaging the
engine cylinders which can set you back
over
$4,000 but don't worry I have a secret
that will help the 10th symptom of a bad
MAF sensor is the check engine light I

when the RPMs drop the sensor value

alcohol move the bag to ensure the

alternatively there's a great product

formula mass airflow sensor cleaner is

it's a little pricier than rubbing

50 and

videos.title: 6 Things That Keep Your DPF Alive
videos.transcript_text:
Your DPF might be slowly dying right
now, and the scary part, you could be
the one causing the damage without even
realizing it. Most diesel owners end up
replacing their DPF somewhere between
100,000 and 150,000 mi. And when they
do, it's a painful hit to the wallet,
usually between $3,000.
But what if I told you there are simple
driving habits and maintenance steps
that can make your DPF last twice as
long, or maybe even longer?
That's exactly what we're talking about
today. In this video, I'm breaking down
the biggest DPF killers and the
surprisingly easy habits that will keep
your filter alive and healthy. No, I'm
not talking about spending money on
expensive additives or chasing
complicated maintenance hacks. This is
about truly understanding how your DPF
works and giving it what it needs to
survive. And make sure you stick around
until the very end because I'm also
going to expose the number one mistake
diesel owners make, the one thing that
cuts your DPF's life in half. So, before
we jump into the solutions, let's take a
closer look at what's actually killing
your DPF, how the DPF works, and why it
fails. Think of your DPF as a super fine
soot trap. Its whole job is to capture
the tiny black particles from your
diesel exhaust so they don't end up in
the air. Now, here's where it gets
interesting. Your DPF isn't just a trap,
it also has a built-in self-cleaning
process called regeneration. During
regeneration, the system cranks up the
heat inside your exhaust to crazy
levels, over 1,100° F,
and burns off the trapped soot. That
soot then turns into fine ash, which
gets blown out through the exhaust.
Sounds perfect, right? Well, not
exactly. Here's the critical problem.
Every single regeneration cycle leaves
behind a little bit of ash that never
goes away. Over time, that microscopic
ash builds up inside the filter.
Slowly but surely, it clogs the DPF,
restricts air flow, and makes future
regenerations less and less effective.
Eventually, you hit the point where the
filter is so loaded with ash that
regeneration can't keep up anymore.
That's what we call DPF death. So,
here's the secret to making your DPF
last. It's not about avoiding
regeneration. You can't. It's about
making sure regeneration happens the
right way, as efficiently and completely
as possible, while also cutting down the
amount of soot your engine produces in
the first place. And that's exactly what
we're going to cover next, specific
practical habits you can start today
that will literally double your DPF's
lifespan. Practice number one, driving
habits that support regeneration. Here's
a big one most diesel owners never think
about. How you drive has a direct impact
on how long your DPF lasts. If most of
your driving is short trips, stop-and-go
traffic, or slow city runs, your engine
never gets hot enough to burn soot
properly. That means your DPF keeps
filling up and regeneration either
doesn't happen at all or happens
halfway, leaving behind extra ash every
time. Think of it like trying to cook
something but shutting the oven off
halfway through.
You don't just get half-cooked food, you
also mess up the oven in the process.
Same deal with your DPF. So, what's the
solution? You've got to give your truck
or SUV some time on the open road. Most
guides say 20 to 30 minutes at speeds
above 40 mph is enough. That's better
than nothing, but here's the truth, for
a full healthy regeneration, you need at
least one solid hour of steady highway
driving every single week. And here's
the kicker, don't baby your engine
during these runs. Keep your RPMs
between 2,000 and 3,000. That's the
sweet spot where your exhaust flow and
temperature hit the levels needed to
clean the filter properly. I call it DPF
exercise. Just like your body needs
regular workouts to stay healthy, your
DPF needs regular highway sessions to
stay alive. Do this and you'll notice
smoother performance, fewer warning
lights, and way less stress on the whole
emission system. Skip it and your DPF
will slowly choke itself to death.
Practice number two, use low ash engine
oil and change it often. Here's a fact
most drivers don't realize, your motor
oil directly affects your DPF's life.
Standard oils contain metallic additives
that when burned turn into ash. And
where does that ash end up? Right inside
your DPF, where it can't ever be
removed. Over time, that ash clogs the
filter and kills it faster than anything
else. That's why smart diesel owners
always use low SAPS oil. SAPS stands for
sulfated ash, phosphorus, and sulfur.
Oils with this label are specially
designed to produce far less ash when
burned, which means your DPF stays
cleaner for longer. But it's not just
about what kind of oil you use, it's
also about how often you change it.
Sure, the manufacturer might tell you
oil can last 10,000 mi or more, but by
then, your oil is already breaking down,
creating more soot, and even mixing with
unburned fuel during failed
regenerations. That's a recipe for
disaster. A better rule, change your oil
every 6,000 to 8,000 mi.
Some mechanics even push for every 5,000
if you do a lot of short trips. Think of
it like this, clean oil, clean
combustion. Clean combustion, fewer
regenerations. Fewer regenerations, less
ash in the DPF. That's how a simple oil
change can save you thousands of dollars
down the road. Practice number three,
fix engine problems right away. Here's a
secret most people miss. The DPF almost
never fails on its own.
When it goes bad, it's usually because
something else in the engine isn't
working right. Think about it, your DPF
is just a filter. If your engine is
running clean, the filter has an easy
job, but if your engine is running
dirty, the DPF gets buried in soot and
ash way too fast. Here are the biggest
culprits, bad fuel injectors. They spray
too much or too little fuel, which means
incomplete combustion. In plain English,
more soot, less power, and a DPF that's
suffocating. Clogged EGR valves. These
stop exhaust gases from flowing
correctly, which ruins the regeneration
process. Air leaks in the intake mess up
the air-fuel mix and create, you guessed
it, more soot. Oil consumption. If your
engine burns oil, that oil turns into
ash inside the DPF. And remember, ash
never goes away. Once it's in there,
it's stuck for good. Bad sensors. A dead
DPF pressure sensor, exhaust temp
sensor, or air flow sensor
can prevent regeneration from even
happening. The rule of thumb, any
problem that makes your engine less
efficient will shorten your DPF's life.
That's why mechanics jump on leaks,
smoke, or warning lights right away.
They know ignoring these issues doesn't
just lead to engine trouble, it also
silently destroys the DPF. So, if you
ever notice odd smells, rough idling,
poor fuel economy, or glowing check
engine light, don't wait. Get it fixed
before your filter takes the hit.
Practice number four, avoid mods that
kill your DPF. A lot of diesel owners
love chasing more horsepower, and sure
it's tempting to slap on a cheap tuning
box or get an aggressive ECU remap, but
here's the ugly truth. Most of those
quick fix mods dump way too much fuel
into your engine. What happens when you
drown the engine in extra fuel? Simple,
it doesn't all burn. That unburned fuel
turns into huge clouds of soot. And
where does that soot go? Straight into
your DPF, clogging it faster than
anything else. Here's what to keep in
mind, cheap tuning boxes soot factories.
They fool your engine into dumping more
fuel without adjusting anything else.
Your DPF pays the price. Aggressive ECU
remaps can also be dangerous if done by
the wrong person.
If the tuner doesn't balance air-fuel
ratios correctly, you'll get extra smoke
and a much shorter DPF life. Even
aftermarket performance air filters can
be a problem. Some let in more dirt than
they should, and others mess with the
mass air flow sensor. That sensor is
critical for proper combustion, and if
it gets confused, you get more soot. And
don't get me started on random additives
or or oil treatments. If they contain
metallic compounds, they create extra
ash that your DPF can never get rid of.
The bottom line, if you really want more
power, pay for a professional tune from
someone who understands DPF systems.
They'll adjust fueling, air flow, and
timing so your engine makes more power
without turning your DPF into a soot
trap. Remember, every shortcut you take
with mods shortens your filter's life.
Practice number five, use quality fuel
and keep the fuel system clean. Your
diesel engine is only as healthy as the
fuel you put into it. And when it comes
to your DPF, bad fuel is like poison.
Here's the deal, low-quality diesel or
fuel with high sulfur content creates
more soot every time you drive. More

videos.transcript_text:
so a question that's cropped up quite a
few times on videos is how do I know if
my car is running a DPF regeneration
cycle it would be nice if manufacturers
all put little likes or Warnings on the
dashboard to give the driver a clue that
such a process is going on now it's
important because you don't really want
to keep shutting the engine off while
this DPF regeneration is going on
because it will not complete and
essentially it'll be restarting on a
cold engine you'll need to warm it up to
operating temperature and then the
Regeneration can start again and you can
quite easily get into a situation where
the DPF never really quite gets clear
just because you as a driver have kept
shutting the engine off before it
happens and also these repeated failed
attempts at regenerating the DPF can
cause other problems oil dilution is a
problem it's using a lot of extra fuel
to try and clear that filter and some of
that fuel ends up in the oil so the more
that process is happening the more
likely you are to have a problem with
oil
dilution so in this video we're just
going to look at the telltale signs
assuming that your car doesn't tell you
that a regeneration is going on so in
some cars you do have a warning on the
dashboard often though this warning only
comes up when the DPF is in danger of
clogging it's really alerting you as a
driver that there is a potential problem
there so manufacturers really want the
Reg generation cycle to happen almost
imperceptibly in the background so as a
driver you need to be a bit of a
detective you need to be familiar with
your car and what's going on with it so
the telltale signs that a DPF
regeneration is taking place in your
diesel engine if you keep an eye on the
miles per gallon if you keep your trip
computer up showing you the current
miles per gallon if you notice that's
suddenly dropping that is a Telltale
sign that the DPF regeneration has
started it will use a lot more fuel dur
in that regeneration cycle is trying to
achieve much higher engine temperatures
and part of the way it does that is by
pushing extra fuel through into the
exhaust stream that goes into the filter
so that that can raise the temperatures
of the filter effectively burning off
the soot particles that have collected
there the next Telltale sign is really a
consequence of this process of cleaning
the engine is running much hotter so you
might notice the temperature gauge
starting to creep up you might notice
that the engine smell
hotter particularly if you park it up
you may notice that the whole engine bay
is just emanating heat you can hear that
ticking noise as the metal is cooling so
that might be an indication that a DPF
regeneration has taken place but also
the cooling fans on the engine are going
to be working extra hard to keep those
temperatures down so if the cooling fans
cut in and that's not something that
normally happens on that part of the
drive at that speed at that RPM then you
can assume that the DPF regeneration is
taking place and and then finally you've
generally got a higher tick over so if
your engine typically idled at say 800
RPMs and you suddenly find it's trying
to idle at 1,000 RPMs that would be the
case in a lot of the Volkswagen group
TDI engine that would be an indication
that the car is trying to run a
regeneration cycle so just being aware
of how the engine works normally and
noticing any differences from that
accepted Norm will alert you as a driver
to the possibility that there is a DPF
regeneration taking place and if that is
the case try not to prematurely stop it
allow that regeneration cycle to
complete it might mean taking a few
extra miles on the journey to extend the
opportunity the car has of clearing that
DPF but it will really help the
long-term prospect it's not a major
problem to interrupt the DPF cycle on
occasions but if you're doing it all the
time that could lead to other problems
where you have to do a forced
regeneration on the DPS itself so
hopefully that's answered the question
please let me know in the comments what

regeneration do you get a warning on the
dashboard do you notice the higher
temperature the engine's running at the
higher tick over or the increased fuel
consumption or is it different in your
car are you really struggling to tell if
that regeneration is taking place so
